Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

practical adjective

concerned with doing, not theory

also in practice, practical experience, hands-on, a practical person

classical

Cic. Off. 1.147: doctōs hominēs vel ūsū perītōs (Lewis & Short, s.v. perītus)

ūsū perītus

phrase: perītus with the ablative ūsū

practised, experienced (of a person)

Ūsus is practice and experience, as against learning (doctrīna); ūsū discere is to learn by doing.

Other words

  • ad ūsum vītae pertinēns — of practical use in life

    phrase · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 3.22 (M-O s.v. practical)

    Of things: useful in daily life, as against what is only theory.

  • āctīvus, āctīva, āctīvum — practical, as against contemplative

    adjective · also used · post-classical · Sen. Ep. 95.10 (Lewis & Short); Quint. 2.18.5 (Lewis & Short)

    A philosophers’ and rhetoricians’ term (Seneca, Quintilian); it is not used of an energetic person (see active).

  • 1The quantity of the first a is not settled: Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked, and the Greek πρᾱκτικός would make it long. Left unmarked.

    practicus1, practica, practicum — active, practical

    adjective · avoid · late Latin · Fulg. Myth. 2.1 (Lewis & Short)

    The Greek πρακτικός in one late author; Seneca and Quintilian say āctīvus.

Examples

  • philosophia et contemplātīva est et āctīva; spectat simul agitque

    philosophy is both theoretical and practical: it looks and at the same time actsSen. Ep. 95.10 (Lewis & Short)

  • Hoc ūsū magis quam librīs didicit.

    He learnt this by doing it rather than from books.composed

See also useful, experience, active, familiar.

SourcesLewis & Short: peritus · Lewis & Short: usus · Lewis & Short: activus · Lewis & Short: practicus

Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. practical.
